html:
This chapter does three things. First it reads the paper: how the 75 marks are built and which unit carried how many marks in the board papers that could be obtained. Second, it gives two complete model papers set exactly to the board's grid — Botany 37 marks, Zoology 38 marks — each with a full solution in the wording and depth of a full-mark answer. Third, it lists over forty ranked predicted questions, each with the reason for the ranking and a short model answer. Sit each paper in three hours without opening the solutions; mark yourself strictly by the brackets.

The grid in one line

Section I Botany 37 = MCQ 5×1 + short 4×4 + long 2×8. Section II Zoology 38 = MCQ 6×1 + short 4×4 + long 2×8. Total 75. The paper has four "OR" choices: one Botany short (Q7 or Q8), Botany Q11, Zoology Q19 (once Q18) and Zoology Q23. Botany and Zoology are answered in separate sections of the same answer sheet, Botany first. The MCQs (Q1–5 and Q12–17) are handed out 30 minutes after the start.

What the data are, and what they are not

The pattern analysis below rests on four full papers: the 2079 board paper (set N), the official 2079 model question, the 2081 board paper (set W) and the 2082 board paper (set M), plus the MCQs of 2080 (Botany) and 2081 (set V). The 2080 paper could not be obtained in full. Four papers are a small sample: they show the board's habits; they do not guarantee the next paper. Every predicted question says why it is on the list, and none is a leak. The curriculum publishes no mark grid by unit, so the unit weights below are measured from those papers and compared with the teaching hours in the syllabus.

10.1 Reading the paper: marks, minutes and order of attack

Part Questions Marks Minutes at 2.4 per mark
Section I Botany, Group A Q1–5, MCQ 5 6
Section I Botany, Group B Q6–9, four shorts 16 38
Section I Botany, Group C Q10–11, two longs 16 38
Section II Zoology, Group A Q12–17, MCQ 6 7
Section II Zoology, Group B Q18–21, four shorts 16 38
Section II Zoology, Group C Q22–23, two longs 16 38
Reading, choosing the ORs, checking 15
  1. Choose the ORs in the first ten minutes. Four OR choices means you always have a question you know better. Write the choice on the question paper.
  2. Draw first. Every long question that says "with diagram" has a separate 2–3 marks for the diagram. Draw it at half a page, label with straight lines, and write the heading.
  3. Write to the brackets. [1+3] means 1 mark for the definition and 3 for the explanation; give the definition its own first line.
  4. Do not leave MCQs blank. There is no negative marking; rewrite the correct option (the letter and the words).
  5. Keep the 15-minute reserve for the diagram labels and for any question you marked with a cross.

10.2 Pattern analysis

In the model paper Botany Q7 was a figure question whose diagram could not be seen; its 4 marks are shown as unassigned. Two things stand out. First, the allocation is remarkably steady: units 1, 6 and 7 carried exactly 5 marks in every paper. Second, Human Biology alone carries about 16–17 of the 38 Zoology marks (about 44 %), which is almost exactly its share of the Zoology teaching hours (28 of 64 hours), and Genetics plus Plant Physiology carry about 23 of the 37 Botany marks (62 %) against 41 of 64 hours.

10.2.2 The long questions: the board's rotation

Paper Botany Q10 Botany Q11 (OR) Zoology Q22 Zoology Q23 (OR)

model 2079 EMP pathway — Physiology Replication (OR crossing over) — Genetics Typhoid — Applied Digestion (OR CO₂ transport) — Human Biology

The rotation is almost mechanical. Botany has one Physiology long and one Genetics long in every paper (4 of 4). Zoology Q22 is a bacterial disease every time (4 of 4: cholera, typhoid, typhoid, tuberculosis) and Q23 is a labelled organ system every time (4 of 4). No long question has yet come from Plant Anatomy, Embryology, Biotechnology, Animal Tissues, Developmental Biology or Population and Health. The four units that carry the long questions are therefore Plant Physiology, Genetics, Human Biology and Applied Biology, and inside them the topics not yet set as a long question are the best guess for the next paper.

10.2.4 Question types and what the marker wants

  • MCQ (11 marks): Botany MCQs rotate over Anatomy, Physiology, Genetics, Embryology and Biotechnology, one each; Zoology MCQs cover Tissues, Development, Human Biology (two or three), Health and Applied Biology. Since 2081 the stems are short application stories.
  • Figure questions (Q7, Q19, Q20, Q23): "study the given figure", label A–D, give a function. Practise the eye, ear, pituitary, nephron, embryo sac, pollen grain and grafting until you can name four parts without thinking.
  • Opinion questions (Q9, Q21): "justify", "plan", "in your view". Give two concrete points and one reason each.

10.3 Model question paper I

Model Question Paper I — Biology (Sub. Code 2021)

NEB-XII Model Set I. Time: 3 hrs. Full marks: 75. Candidates are required to give their answers in their own words as far as practicable. The figures in the margin indicate full marks. Attempt all the questions. Complete Section I (Botany) first and then Section II (Zoology); answer each section separately in the same answer sheet.

Section I: Botany

Group A — Rewrite the correct option of each question. 5 × 1 = 5

  1. Which one of the following is a function of the endodermis of the root? [1]aphotosynthesisbregulating the movement of water and minerals into the stelecsecondary growth of the rootdconduction of food
  2. In a C4 plant, which enzyme first fixes atmospheric CO₂ in the mesophyll cells? [1]aRuBisCObPEP carboxylasecATP synthasedpyruvate kinase
  3. The F₂ phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross with complete dominance is [1]a3 : 1b1 : 2 : 1c9 : 3 : 3 : 1d1 : 1 : 1 : 1
  4. A pollen grain with a thick exine of sporopollenin is produced in the [1]aovulebanthercstigmadstyle
  5. Virus-free plantlets can be obtained by culturing [1]aleaf segmentsbroot tips onlycshoot-apex meristemdmature pollen

Group B — Short answer questions. 4 × 4 = 16

  1. Differentiate between xylem and phloem on the basis of cell types, living or dead condition, material conducted and direction of conduction. [4]
  2. Study the given figure of a vascular bundle and answer the questions. [1+2+1] (i) Identify the type of vascular bundle in the figure. (ii) Name the parts A to D. (iii) State the function of part B.
  3. State Mendel's law of segregation and explain it with a monohybrid cross up to F₂. [1+3] OR Describe four physiological effects of auxin in plants. [4]
  4. Explain how Bt cotton is produced and discuss two benefits and two concerns of its use. [2+2]

Group C — Long answer questions. 2 × 8 = 16

  1. Describe the Krebs cycle. How many NADH, FADH₂ and ATP molecules are formed from one molecule of glucose in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle? [1+5+2]
  2. State and explain Mendel's law of independent assortment with the help of a dihybrid cross. Show the F₂ phenotypic and genotypic ratios. [1+5+2] OR "Genes are expressed as proteins." Explain the processes of transcription and translation with necessary diagrams. [2+3+3]

Section II: Zoology

Group A — Rewrite the correct option of each question. 6 × 1 = 6

  1. Which cells of the blood produce antibodies? [1]aneutrophilsbplasma cellsceosinophilsdplatelets
  2. The hormone that lowers the blood glucose level is [1]aglucagonbadrenalinecinsulindcortisol
  3. Fertilisation in the human female normally takes place in the [1]auterusbampulla of the fallopian tubeccervixdovary
  4. Ultrafiltration of blood takes place in the [1]aproximal convoluted tubulebloop of Henlecglomerulus and Bowman's capsuledcollecting duct
  5. Deficiency of vitamin A causes [1]ascurvybnight blindnesscricketsdberi-beri
  6. Which of the following diseases is caused by a protozoan? [1]atyphoidbtuberculosiscmalariadcholera

Group B — Short answer questions. 4 × 4 = 16

  1. Differentiate between bone and cartilage on the basis of matrix, cells, blood supply and location. [4]
  2. Study the given figure of a neuron and answer the questions. [1+1+2] (i) Name the parts A and B. (ii) What is the direction of the nerve impulse in a neuron? (iii) Explain the role of part D and part C in the transmission of the impulse. OR Describe gastrulation in the frog. [4]
  3. Explain how the hormones insulin and glucagon regulate the blood glucose level. Name one disorder of their imbalance. [3+1]
  4. What is AIDS? Describe how HIV spreads and how it can be prevented. [1+1.5+1.5]

Group C — Long answer questions. 2 × 8 = 16

  1. Name the causative agent of malaria. Describe its life cycle in man and in the mosquito. Mention the symptoms and control measures. [1+3+2+2]
  2. Draw a labelled diagram of the human heart in longitudinal section and describe the double circulation of blood. [3+3+2] OR Draw a labelled neuron. Explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted along an axon. [2+3+3]

10.4 Solutions to Model Question Paper I

Answer key — Group A (Botany 1–5, Zoology 12–17)

1. (b) — the root endodermis, through its Casparian strips and living cells, decides what enters the stele. Option (d) belongs to phloem, and the starch-storing endodermis is the stem's.

2. (b) — PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll fixes CO₂ as oxaloacetate; RuBisCO works later in the bundle sheath. Choosing RuBisCO is the C3 reflex.

3. (c) — 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Option (a) is the monohybrid ratio.

4. (b) — pollen grains form in the anther, from microspore mother cells.

5. (c) — the shoot-apex meristem is free of virus; leaf pieces and roots carry it.

12. (b) — plasma cells (differentiated B lymphocytes) make antibodies; eosinophils and neutrophils are phagocytes or parasite-killers.

13. (c) — insulin (β cells) lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.

14. (b) — fertilisation occurs in the ampulla; implantation, not fertilisation, is in the uterus.

15. (c) — pressure filtration through the glomerular capillaries and Bowman's capsule; the PCT reabsorbs.

16. (b) — vitamin A is needed for rhodopsin; scurvy is vitamin C, rickets vitamin D, beri-beri vitamin B₁.

17. (c) — malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan; the other three are bacterial.

Solutions — Section I Botany, Group B (6–9)

6.

Basis Xylem Phloem
Cell types tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, phloem parenchyma
Living or dead mostly dead (only the parenchyma lives); walls lignified mostly living (phloem fibres are dead); walls of cellulose
Material conducted water and dissolved minerals prepared food (sucrose) and hormones
Direction upward only (root → leaf) up and down (source → sink)

7. (i) An open collateral vascular bundle, as in a dicot stem: xylem and phloem lie on the same radius, with a strip of cambium between them. [1] (ii) A = phloem (sieve tubes and companion cells); B = cambium; C = metaxylem (large vessels); D = protoxylem (small vessels, towards the pith: the xylem is endarch). [2] (iii) B, the cambium, is a meristem; it divides to cut secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward, so the stem grows in girth. [1]

8. Law [1]. The two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) when gametes form, so each gamete receives only one allele of the pair; the two alleles meet again at random at fertilisation. Monohybrid cross [3]. Pure tall (TT) × pure dwarf (tt) → all F₁ tall (Tt). F₁ self-crossed: gametes T and t from each parent.

T t
T TT tall Tt tall
t Tt tall tt dwarf

F₂: 3 tall : 1 dwarf (phenotypic); 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (genotypic). The recessive trait reappears unchanged in one quarter of the F₂, which shows that the alleles did not blend but separated. OR — effects of auxin [4]. (i) Cell elongation in the stem, so shoots grow and bend towards light (phototropism). (ii) Apical dominance: the shoot tip suppresses the lateral buds. (iii) Root initiation on cuttings (IBA, NAA). (iv) Parthenocarpy and prevention of fruit drop; 2,4-D is a selective weed-killer of broad-leaved weeds.

9. Production [2]. The cry gene of Bacillus thuringiensis, which codes for an insecticidal Cry protein, is cut out with a restriction enzyme and inserted in the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Cotton cells or explants are infected; the cells that took up the gene are selected on antibiotic medium and regenerated into plants by tissue culture, then tested in the field. In the bollworm's alkaline gut the protoxin is activated, binds to the gut wall and kills the larva. Benefits [1] and concerns [1]. Benefits: less insecticide spraying, lower cost and less poisoning of farmers, higher yield. Concerns: pests may evolve resistance, non-target insects may be harmed, genes may flow to wild relatives, and the seed is patented and costly.

Solutions — Section I Botany, Group C (10–11)

10. Krebs cycle [1 + 5]. Sir Hans Krebs described it in 1937. It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and is a cycle because oxaloacetate is regenerated. Each pyruvate from glycolysis first enters the link reaction: pyruvate + NAD⁺ + CoA → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH. (1) Acetyl CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) (citrate synthase). (2) Citrate → isocitrate (aconitase). (3) Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (5C) + CO₂ + NADH. (4) α-Ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA (4C) + CO₂ + NADH. (5) Succinyl CoA → succinate + GTP (→ ATP), substrate-level phosphorylation. (6) Succinate → fumarate + FADH₂. (7) Fumarate → malate. (8) Malate → oxaloacetate + NADH. One turn: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (GTP). Yield per glucose [2].

Stage NADH FADH₂ ATP CO₂
Link reaction (2 pyruvate) 2 0 0 2
Krebs cycle (2 turns) 6 2 2 4
Total 8 2 2 6

In the electron transport system the 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂ give about 20 + 3 = 23 ATP (2.5 and 1.5 ATP each); adding 2 ATP gives about 25 ATP from these two stages, and with glycolysis the total is 30–32 ATP per glucose (36–38 in older books).

11. Law [1]. When two or more pairs of contrasting characters are followed together, the alleles of each gene assort independently into the gametes, so the inheritance of one character does not affect that of another. Dihybrid cross [5]. Pure round yellow seeds (RRYY) × pure wrinkled green (rryy) → F₁ all round yellow (RrYy). The F₁ makes four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY, ry. Selfing the F₁ (4 × 4 = 16 combinations):

RY Ry rY ry
RY RRYY round yellow RRYy round yellow RrYY round yellow RrYy round yellow
Ry RRYy round yellow RRyy round green RrYy round yellow Rryy round green
rY RrYY round yellow RrYy round yellow rrYY wrinkled yellow rrYy wrinkled yellow
ry RrYy round yellow Rryy round green rrYy wrinkled yellow rryy wrinkled green

Ratios [2]. Phenotypic: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. Genotypic: 1 RRYY : 2 RRYy : 2 RrYY : 4 RrYy : 1 RRyy : 2 Rryy : 1 rrYY : 2 rrYy : 1 rryy (nine genotypes). Two new combinations — round green and wrinkled yellow — appear, which shows that the two characters were inherited independently. OR — transcription and translation [2+3+3]. Gene expression is the flow DNA → mRNA → protein. Transcription (in the nucleus): RNA polymerase binds the promoter, the DNA opens, and the template strand (3′→5′) is copied into a complementary mRNA 5′→3′ (A–U, T–A, G–C, C–G) until the terminator; in eukaryotes the primary transcript is spliced (introns out), capped and given a poly-A tail. Translation (on ribosomes in the cytoplasm): the small ribosomal subunit binds mRNA at the AUG start codon; the initiator tRNA (Met) pairs with it; each further codon is matched by a tRNA whose anticodon is complementary and which carries the right amino acid; peptide bonds join the amino acids (elongation) as the ribosome moves along the mRNA; a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) makes the ribosome release the protein. Diagrams [3]. (a) DNA, RNA polymerase and the mRNA strand; (b) ribosome with mRNA, tRNA and the growing polypeptide.

Solutions — Section II Zoology, Group B (18–21)

18.

Basis Bone Cartilage
Matrix hard, of calcium phosphate and collagen firm but flexible, of chondroitin sulphate and collagen
Cells osteocytes in lacunae, linked by canaliculi chondrocytes in lacunae (singly or in groups)
Blood supply rich: blood vessels run in the Haversian canals none (avascular); fed by diffusion from the perichondrium
Location skeleton: limbs, skull, vertebrae nose, ear pinna, trachea, ends of long bones, intervertebral discs

19. (i) A = dendrites; B = cell body (cyton) with the nucleus. [1] (ii) The impulse travels in one direction only: dendrite → cell body → axon → axon terminal. [1] (iii) C is the axon (here a myelinated one): it conducts the impulse away from the cell body as an action potential; the myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier makes the impulse jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is faster. D is the synaptic knob (axon terminal): it holds vesicles of neurotransmitter (acetylcholine), which it releases into the synaptic cleft when the impulse arrives, so that the impulse passes to the next neuron or to a muscle. [2] OR — gastrulation in the frog [4]. After blastulation the dorsal lip of the blastopore appears near the grey crescent. Cells of the animal hemisphere spread over the surface (epiboly) and roll inward over the lip (invagination and involution), forming the archenteron, which enlarges as the blastocoel shrinks. The large yolky cells left in the blastopore form the yolk plug. By the end, ectoderm outside, endoderm lining the archenteron and mesoderm between them are formed.

20. Both hormones come from the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas; they work as opposites in a negative feedback loop. Insulin [1.5]. When blood glucose rises after a meal, the β cells release insulin; it makes muscle and fat cells take in glucose and makes the liver convert glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis), so blood glucose falls. Glucagon [1.5]. When blood glucose falls, the α cells release glucagon; it makes the liver break glycogen to glucose (glycogenolysis) and make new glucose from amino acids (gluconeogenesis), so blood glucose rises. Disorder [1]. Too little insulin, or cells that do not respond to it, causes diabetes mellitus (high blood sugar, glucose in urine, thirst, weight loss); too much insulin causes hypoglycaemia (shaking, sweating, fainting).

21. AIDS [1]. Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, caused by HIV, an RNA retrovirus that destroys CD4 helper T cells. Spread [1.5]. Unprotected sexual intercourse; transfusion of infected blood or use of shared needles and razors; from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breast-feeding. It does not spread by touch, mosquito bite, food or shared toilets. Prevention [1.5]. Faithfulness and condom use; screened blood only; single-use syringes; antiretroviral drugs for infected mothers; education and counselling.

Solutions — Section II Zoology, Group C (22–23)

22. Causative agent [1]. Plasmodium (P. vivax and P. falciparum are the important species), a protozoan carried by the female Anopheles. Life cycle [3]. In man: sporozoites injected by the mosquito go to the liver and multiply (schizogony); the merozoites enter red cells and multiply again, and the cells burst every 48 hours, releasing toxin and more merozoites; some become gametocytes. In the mosquito: the mosquito takes up gametocytes with the blood; male and female gametes fuse in its gut; the zygote (ookinete) forms an oocyst on the gut wall, which releases sporozoites into the salivary glands. Symptoms [2]. Periodic chills, high fever and sweating; headache and vomiting; anaemia and enlarged spleen; cerebral malaria in severe falciparum infection. Control [2]. Destroy breeding places (drain stagnant water), indoor residual spraying, larvicides and larvivorous fish; insecticide-treated bed nets and repellents; rapid diagnosis and treatment with artemisinin-based drugs.

23. Diagram [3]. Draw the heart in longitudinal section and label: right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle, tricuspid valve, bicuspid (mitral) valve, semilunar valves, superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta, interventricular septum. (Use the figure below as a model.)

Double circulation [3]. Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit. Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → arteries → capillaries of the body (oxygen given up) → veins → superior and inferior vena cava → right atrium. Pulmonary circulation: right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → pulmonary artery (deoxygenated blood) → lungs (oxygen taken up) → pulmonary veins → left atrium → (bicuspid valve) → left ventricle. Significance [2]. The oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix, so the tissues get fully oxygenated blood; the body circuit can keep a high pressure while the lung circuit has a low pressure; this suits warm-blooded animals that need much energy. OR — neuron and nerve impulse [2+3+3]. Neuron [2]. Cell body (cyton) with nucleus and Nissl granules; dendrites that receive; a long axon, wrapped in a myelin sheath from Schwann cells with gaps called nodes of Ranvier; ends in synaptic knobs. Generation [3]. At rest the membrane is polarised at about −70 mV (more Na⁺ outside, more K⁺ inside, kept by the Na⁺–K⁺ pump). A stimulus opens Na⁺ channels; Na⁺ rushes in and the inside becomes positive (depolarisation, about +35 mV): the action potential. Then K⁺ channels open, K⁺ leaves and the membrane returns to −70 mV (repolarisation). Conduction [3]. The action potential depolarises the next patch of membrane, so it travels as a wave; in a myelinated axon it jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), reaching up to 100 m s⁻¹. It follows the all-or-none law. At the synapse the impulse is carried by neurotransmitter.

10.6 Solutions to Model Question Paper II

Answer key — Group A (Botany 1–5, Zoology 12–17)

1. (c) — cork cambium is a lateral meristem. Shoot and root apices are apical, and the intercalary meristem is in grass internodes.

2. (c) — abscisic acid, the stress hormone, closes stomata. Gibberellin and cytokinin tend to keep them open.

3. (b) — a transition is purine→purine or pyrimidine→pyrimidine; a transversion swaps the classes (option a).

8. Cohesion–tension theory [3]. Proposed by Dixon and Joly (1894). Water is lost by transpiration from the leaf mesophyll, creating a tension (negative pressure) in the leaf xylem. Because water molecules cohere to each other (hydrogen bonds) and adhere to the xylem walls, the water column, unbroken from leaf to root, is pulled up as a continuous stream; the tension can reach many atmospheres, enough for the tallest trees. Evidence [1]. The diameter of a tree trunk shrinks slightly by day, when transpiration is at its highest, showing that the xylem is under tension; a cut stem pulls in air or coloured water. OR [4]. Gibberellins: (i) stretch the internodes (bolting) and make dwarf plants tall; (ii) break seed and bud dormancy and promote germination of cereals (barley malting); (iii) produce seedless, larger grapes. Cytokinins: (i) promote cell division (with auxin) and shoot formation in tissue culture; (ii) delay leaf senescence; (iii) break apical dominance. (Any two of each.)

9. Biofertilisers [1] and green manure [1], with examples [2]. A biofertiliser is a living microorganism that increases soil fertility or the nutrient supply of a plant: Rhizobium for legumes, Azotobacter for cereals, Azolla with Anabaena for rice fields, phosphate-solubilising bacteria. Green manure is a crop grown and ploughed into the soil while still green to add organic matter and nitrogen: Sesbania (dhaincha), Crotalaria (sunhemp). Sustainability. They replace costly imported chemical fertiliser, improve soil structure and water holding capacity, avoid soil and water pollution, and keep the soil microbes alive.

Solutions — Section I Botany, Group C (10–11)

10. Introduction [1]. The C4 pathway, worked out by Hatch and Slack (1966), is a carbon-concentrating mechanism in plants such as maize and sugarcane. Kranz anatomy. The leaf shows two types of photosynthetic cells: mesophyll cells and, round every vein, a ring of large bundle-sheath cells with big chloroplasts — the Kranz ("wreath") arrangement. Pathway [5]. 1. In the mesophyll. CO₂ enters as bicarbonate; PEP carboxylase joins it to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP, 3C) to form oxaloacetate (OAA, 4C), the first stable product. PEP carboxylase has no affinity for O₂. 2. OAA is converted to malate (or aspartate), which moves through plasmodesmata into the bundle sheath. 3. In the bundle sheath. Malate is decarboxylated: CO₂ is released at a high concentration and pyruvate (3C) is left. 4. The CO₂ enters the normal Calvin cycle: RuBisCO fixes it, because the local CO₂ is so high that RuBisCO acts as a carboxylase and photorespiration is almost suppressed. 5. Pyruvate returns to the mesophyll, where pyruvate phosphate dikinase (using 2 ATP equivalents) regenerates PEP. Efficiency [2]. In hot, dry air the stomata partly close, the leaf CO₂ falls and O₂ rises, which makes RuBisCO in C3 plants waste carbon in photorespiration. The C4 plant pumps CO₂ into the bundle sheath, so it keeps photosynthesising at a high temperature (30–45 °C) with stomata closed, loses less water per gram of dry matter and has a higher yield, though at an extra cost of 2 ATP per CO₂.

11. Linkage [1]. The tendency of genes that lie on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Morgan's experiment [4]. Morgan crossed a grey-bodied, long-winged fly (b⁺b⁺ vg⁺vg⁺) with a black-bodied, vestigial-winged fly (bb vgvg); the F₁ were all grey and long. He test-crossed an F₁ female with a black vestigial male (bb vgvg) and expected 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 if the genes assorted independently. He got 965 grey long : 944 black vestigial : 206 grey vestigial : 185 black long. Parental types were 83 % and recombinants 17 %, so the genes were linked on the same chromosome; the few recombinants showed that linkage is incomplete. How crossing over breaks linkage [1]. In prophase I of meiosis in the heterozygous female, non-sister chromatids of the homologues exchange segments at pachytene; the gametes Bvg and bVg⁺ carry new combinations, so the grey vestigial and black long flies appear. No crossing over occurs in male Drosophila, which is why a female is used. Significance [2]. It produces variation, it makes gene maps possible (1 % recombination = 1 map unit), and it lets breeders combine useful genes. OR — types of RNA [2+6]. RNA is a single-stranded polymer of ribonucleotides containing ribose and uracil; it is made on a DNA template by transcription. mRNA (messenger) — about 5 % of cellular RNA; copies the gene; each three bases form a codon; it carries the message to the ribosome. tRNA (transfer) — clover-leaf, 75–90 nucleotides, with an anticodon loop and an amino-acid attachment site at the 3′ end; it reads the codon and brings the matching amino acid. rRNA (ribosomal) — the commonest RNA (~80 %); with proteins it forms the two ribosomal subunits, the site of translation, and catalyses peptide-bond formation. In protein synthesis: mRNA is made in the nucleus and moves to the cytoplasm; the ribosome (rRNA) binds it at AUG; tRNAs bring amino acids in the order the codons dictate; the ribosome joins them by peptide bonds until a stop codon ends the chain. Minor types: snRNA (splicing) and miRNA (gene regulation).

20. The eye focuses by changing the curvature of the lens (accommodation), controlled by the ciliary muscle and the suspensory ligaments. Distant object [1.5]. The ciliary muscle relaxes, the suspensory ligaments tighten and pull the lens flat; its focal length rises, so parallel rays focus on the retina. Near object [1.5]. The ciliary muscle contracts, the ligaments slacken, the lens becomes thicker and rounder (shorter focal length), so diverging rays from a near object focus on the retina; the pupil also constricts. Defect [1]. Myopia (short sight): the eyeball is too long, so distant objects focus in front of the retina; corrected with concave lenses. (Hypermetropia is corrected with convex lenses.)

Solutions — Section II Zoology, Group C (22–23)

22. Causative agent [1]. Hepatitis B virus (HBV), a DNA virus of the family Hepadnaviridae. Transmission [2]. Blood and body fluids: transfusion of infected blood, sharing of needles and razors, unprotected sexual intercourse, and from an infected mother to her baby at birth. It does not spread by food and water (that is hepatitis A and E). Symptoms [2]. After an incubation of 1–6 months: loss of appetite, nausea, fatigue, fever and joint pain, jaundice (yellow skin and eyes), dark urine, pale stools and right-side abdominal pain. Prevention [2]. Hepatitis B vaccine (in Nepal given in the pentavalent vaccine to infants); screening of donated blood; single-use needles and syringes; safe sex; vaccination of newborns of infected mothers; health workers must be vaccinated. Complications [1]. Chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma).

23. Diagram [3]. Draw the outer ear (pinna, auditory canal, tympanic membrane), the middle ear (malleus, incus, stapes, oval window, round window, Eustachian tube) and the inner ear (cochlea, vestibule with utriculus and sacculus, three semicircular canals, auditory nerve). Use the ear figure given in section 9.8 as the model. Hearing [3]. Sound waves are collected by the pinna and travel down the auditory canal to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. The vibrations are passed and amplified by the three ossicles — malleus, incus and stapes — to the oval window. They set the perilymph of the cochlea moving; waves in the fluid move the basilar membrane, and the hair cells of the organ of Corti bend against the tectorial membrane and fire impulses in the auditory nerve to the temporal lobe of the cerebrum, where the sound is perceived. The round window bulges to relieve the pressure; the Eustachian tube equalises the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. Semicircular canals [2]. Three canals in three planes at right angles, each with an ampulla and a crista with hair cells. When the head rotates, the endolymph lags, bends the hair cells and sends impulses through the vestibular nerve to the cerebellum, which adjusts posture: they sense rotation and dynamic balance; the utriculus and sacculus sense static balance and linear movement. OR — urine formation [2+4+2]. Ultrafiltration [2]: in the glomerulus the blood pressure (about 70 mm Hg, high because the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent) forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea through the capillary wall, the basement membrane and the podocytes into Bowman's capsule; proteins and cells stay. About 125 mL a minute (180 L a day) of glomerular filtrate is formed. Selective reabsorption [4]: in the PCT all the glucose and amino acids, most Na⁺, K⁺, HCO₃⁻ and about 65 % of the water are returned to the blood by active and passive transport; the loop of Henle builds a concentration gradient (descending limb loses water, ascending limb pumps out salt); the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water under ADH. About 99 % of the filtrate is reclaimed. Tubular secretion: the DCT secretes H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ and drugs into the tubule, controlling the blood pH and ion balance. The remaining fluid is urine (about 1.5 litres a day). ADH [2]: antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary makes the DCT and collecting duct permeable to water; when the body is short of water more ADH is released and small volumes of concentrated urine result; when there is plenty, less ADH gives copious dilute urine. Too little ADH causes diabetes insipidus.

How the ranking works. A = the unit is certain (it has carried marks in all four papers) and the topic has not yet been set in the slot where the board habitually asks it; B = the topic has appeared only as an OR, a short or an MCQ and has not been the main long question; C = plausible but the unit has been set less regularly.
